search.slidetext: developing and implementing a leak detection and repair (ldar) program to mitigate methane emissions from the oil and gas sector

disclaimer this course is not intended to address applicable national, state, tribal, or local ldar regulations. prior to developing a non-regulatory ldar program, please ensure you understand any relevant ldar regulations that may apply in your jurisdiction.

welcome the united states environmental protection agency (epa) developed this course in support of the global methane initiative (gmi). this course explains the concept, objectives, systematic approach, challenges and benefits of a non-regulatory leak detection and repair (ldar) program for managing methane emissions from equipment leaks at oil and natural gas facilities. in addition, it provides specific guidance on designing, implementing, and managing the ldar program. what is the gmi? what is the gmi? what is the gmi? what is the gmi? what is the gmi? what is the gmi?

module 2 methane leaks from oil and gas equipment
what you will learn in this module, you will learn the following: what are equipment leaks? what are the typical equipment component types that contribute to total leakage?
what are equipment leaks? introduction to equipment leaks definition of an equipment leak based on screening data characteristics of equipment leaks definition of a large leak

introduction to equipment leaks equipment leaks, commonly referred to as fugitive emissions, are unintentional emissions from equipment components. the occurrence of an equipment leak generally indicates that the equipment component needs repair or replacement. examples of equipment leaks detected using an optimal gas imaging (ogi) camera:

definition of an equipment leak based on screening data an equipment leak is typically defined as an equipment component that has: a hydrocarbon gas/vapor screening concentration greater than a certain practical limit (for example, a concentration of greater than or equal to 10,000 ppm as determined using u.s. epa method 21). visible leakage detected using an ogi camera (for example, in accordance with u.s. epa’s appendix k to 40 cfr part 60). learn more about u.s. epa method 21 learn more about u.s. epa method 21 learn more about u.s. epa method 21 learn more about u.s. epa method 21 learn more about u.s. epa method 21 learn more about u.s. epa method 21 learn more about u.s. epa‘s requirements for using optical gas imaging in leak detection learn more about u.s. epa‘s requirements for using optical gas imaging in leak detection learn more about u.s. epa‘s requirements for using optical gas imaging in leak detection learn more about u.s. epa‘s requirements for using optical gas imaging in leak detection learn more about u.s. epa‘s requirements for using optical gas imaging in leak detection learn more about u.s. epa‘s requirements for using optical gas imaging in leak detection

characteristics of equipment leaks companies have found that equipment leaks have the following characteristics at any give time: only a relatively small percentage of the equipment components at a facility tend to leak. most of the emissions from equipment leaks tend to be generated by a few large leaks rather than by many smaller and medium-sized leaks. some equipment components are more leak prone than others depending on their type and operational service: for example, pressure relief valves and open-ended lines are more likely to leak than connectors. according to u.s. epa’s natural gas star program, the likelihood of an equipment component to leak and the average emissions rate when it leaks tends to vary by the segment of the oil and gas industry (https://www.epa.gov/natural-gas-star-program/equipment-leaks). oil and natural gas companies have found that the 10 largest leaks at a site will typically contribute 80% or more of the total emissions from leakage. hence, it is strategic to efficiently find and repair the largest leaks.

characteristics of equipment leaks: potential to leak the likelihood of an equipment component to wear out and leak varies by the type of component and service. equipment components are more likely to leak when used in demanding applications such as vibration, thermal cycling or cryogenic service which causes: increased wear and tear reduced performance of gaskets and packing materials fouling, corrosion, or damage of sealing surfaces leaking equipment components, even after successful repair, may eventually leak again. therefore, ongoing regular inspection and maintenance is highly recommended. equipment components at older facilities are generally more likely to leak.

characteristics of equipment leaks: detectability components in sour or odorized service tend to have fewer emissions over time than those in “sweet” or odorless service, because the leaks are readily detected between ldar surveys by olfactory means and are addressed quickly due to safety concerns. natural gas is considered “sour” if it contains hydrogen sulfide (h2s) and carbon dioxide (co2) in excess of local market specifications.

definition of a large leak while not universally defined, a large leak has a gross economic value of tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of dollars per year or more. for an example with an associated rate, the u.s. epa’s super emitter program considers an emission rate of 100 kilogram per hour (kg/h) of methane or greater to be a large leak (https://www.epa.gov/compliance/methane-super-emitter-program). some reasons for large leaks include: severe or demanding service (e.g., vibration and thermal cycling) prolonged neglect leaks may go unnoticed (e.g., located in infrequently visited or difficult to access areas) a lack of measurement data that would justify repairs based on the magnitude of related health, safety, environmental, operability, and economic-loss concerns
what are the typical equipment component types that contribute to total leakage? equipment component types

equipment component types companies have found that emissions contributions are a function of the average leak rate per component and component count. this section describes different types of common equipment component leak sources1. 1 not all equipment component categories will necessarily apply at all facilities. blowdown systems and open-ended lines thief hatches pressure relief devices valves connectors other equipment components (pressure regulators, flow meters, and mechanically-operated engine fuel injectors)

equipment component type: blowdown systems and open-ended lines (oels) there are typically two types of blowdown systems: (i) whole facility or station and (ii) process unit (e.g., dehydrator, line heater, compressor, treater, etc.). blowdown systems tend to be major sources of emissions due to leakage into the vent header in between blowdown events. leaks at oels commonly occur where drain, injection, or sampling points are provided on process lines and vessels. blowdown systems and oels have one or more valves that are normally closed and pressurized on one side, and on the other side are either open to the atmosphere or connected to a vent system. in these circumstances the leakage is past the seat of the closed valves. typical valve that is the source of leaks in blowdown systems

equipment component type: blowdown systems and open-ended lines (oels) (continued) for blowdown systems the valve is typically greater than or equal to 2” (50 mm) nominal pipe size (nps) and for oels it is less than 2” nps. leakage points the leakage occurs past the seat of the closed valve and discharges to the atmosphere directly or via a vent system. this leakage is either caused by: improper seating of the valve due to the presence of debris on the valve seat prior seat damage or wear left: open-ended line right: capped (controlled) open-ended line globe valve (closed) ball valve (closed)

equipment component type: blowdown systems and open-ended lines (oels) (continued) there are two scenarios in which leakage into a blowdown system may occur. the presented example is for a compressor unit blowdown system: scenario 1: compressor unit pressurized during pressurized conditions, the blowdown valve is closed, and the upstream equipment is pressurized. the leakage occurs past the seat of the closed blowdown valve. scenario 2: compressor unit depressurized during the period in which equipment has been depressurized, the blowdown valve remains open. the leakage is past the seats of the upstream and downstream valves used to isolate the equipment prior to depressurization. leakage rates in scenario 2 tend to be greater than in scenario 1. show diagram show diagram show diagram show diagram show diagram show diagram show diagram show diagram show diagram show diagram show diagram show diagram

equipment component type: thief hatches tank thief hatches are used for sampling product from fixed-roof storage tanks. the hatch normally features a pressure relief mechanism. leakage points thief hatches are a potential sources of leakage in cases where the tank vapor space is pressurized. examples include when the tank is connected to a vapor collection and control system or where the tank features a positive-pressure gas blanketing system (e.g., to preclude air ingress). unintentional gas or vapor losses may occur from thief hatches in these cases due to fouling of the seating surface of the hatch or over-pressure conditions caused by under-sizing of the vapor collection system. tank thief hatch leakage points

equipment component type: pressure relief devices pressure relief devices are used to release an unplanned, nonroutine discharge of gas from process equipment to avoid safety hazards or equipment damage. pressure relief devices include pressure relief valves (prvs), rupture discs, pressure/vacuum vents, etc. prvs are the most common pressure relief devices uses in the oil and gas industry. they are spring-loaded valves used to protect pressure vessels from over-pressurization. leakage points the leakage occurs past the prv seat. this leakage is of greatest environmental concern where the prv relieves directly to atmosphere or into an uncontrolled vent system. potential leakage points associated with pressure relief devices

equipment component type: valves valves are one of the most commonly occurring equipment components at oil and gas facilities. there are two categories of valves: rising stem and quarter-turn valves. rising stem valves: require the valve stem to move vertically up to open and down to close the valve. include gate, globe, and needle valves. quarter-turn valves: require the valve stem to rotate through 90° to go from a fully closed to fully open position. include ball, plug, and butterfly valves. valves are either equipped with a hand wheel or handle for manual operation, or an actuator for automated operation. rising stem valves are more prone to leaks than quarter-turn valves.

equipment component type: valves (continued) valve leakage may occur from the valve body and the valve stem packing. leakage from the valve end connections is classified separately as connector leakage. leakage past the valve seat to the atmosphere is classified as a blowdown system or oel leak. control valves tend to have greater valve-stem leakage potential than block valves. this is because the packing mechanism may be less tight to allow smooth movement of the valve stem for control purposes. control valves also tend to experience greater valve-stem activity levels resulting in increased packing wear and tear. manually operated valves control valve
leakage from commonly used valves rising-stem and quarter-turn valves commonly used at oil and gas facilities.

equipment component type: connectors connectors are mechanical connections typically used to join two pieces of pipe or another type of equipment component to a pipe or vessel. covers, caps, and plugs are considered a type of connection. connectors usually are either threaded, flanged, or clamped. the most common type of connectors are threaded and flanged. leakage points connector leakage occurs past the threads, flange face, or mating surfaces. connectors used on fuel gas systems and vibration and thermal cycling service tend to be more leak prone than other service applications. large leaks from connectors typically occur because they are not properly tightened (human error). top arrows: leakage from a series of threaded hexagonal plugs at the end of two aerial coolers bottom arrows: leakage from two flanges leakage from connectors examples of threaded connections associated with a thermal well and an open-ended bleed valve

equipment component type:pressure regulators pressure regulators are commonly used in a process where pressure regulation is required, such as compressor starter motors, chemical injection pumps, pneumatic controllers, gas blanketing systems, fuel gas systems, etc. leakage points leakage can occur from the regulator body or vent port in pressure regulators.

equipment component type: flow meters flow meters in natural gas and crude oil service are additional potential sources of leakage. leakage points leakage can occur from the various packing glands and connections on the meter body. leakage from the meter end connections is classified as connector leakage. image of an orifice meter

equipment component type: mechanically operated engine fuel injectors mechanically operated fuel injectors are commonly used on older integral compressor drivers and are a potential source of leakage. leakage points leakage can occur from the various fittings on the injector but primarily around the stem of the injector valve.
module 2 summary

what you have learned in this module, you learned about equipment leaks, their characteristics, and reasons for large leaks. in a typical facility, the following equipment components types contribute to total leakage: blowdown systems and open-ended lines thief hatches pressure relief devices valves connectors other equipment components (pressure regulators, flow meters, and mechanically-operated engine fuel injectors) equipment leaks contribute significantly to total methane emissions at natural gas facilities. equipment components at older facilities are generally more likely to leak.

what you have learned (continued) in addition to these sources, companies have found that other equipment components can leak. it is important that operators identify and consider all potential types of leak sources at their facilities. operators should strive to repair all leaks. however, targeting the largest leaks can still make a significant difference in reducing an operator’s emissions since these leaks will tend to contribute the most to the total emissions at a facility. therefore, a practical approach to efficiently manage emissions is to: (i) identify the facilities that have the greatest leakage, and (ii) find and repair the largest leaks at these facilities. equipment leaks in excess of normal tolerances allowed by the equipment manufacturer should be repaired whenever it is economical to do so (i.e., based on direct repair or replacement costs and the value of the product being lost). equipment leaks in excess of applicable health, safety and environment (hs&e) standards should be repaired regardless of the cost.
thank you! you have completed: module 2. methane leaks from oil and gas equipment
